name: La Hougue Bie and Balnuaran of Clava
about: Two passage graves aligned on the sun: La Hougue Bie in Jersey (Neolithic, c. 4000 BC; equinox sunrise along the passage; medieval chapels on top and the lost Prince's Tower, 1792-1924) and the Bronze Age cemetery of Balnuaran of Clava near Inverness (c. 2000 BC; two passage graves facing the midwinter sunset with a ring cairn between, each in a ring of graded standing stones).

la_hougue_bie.name: La Hougue Bie
la_hougue_bie.record_note: Q1395892 is a place (table places), not a buildings row; there is no catalogue building for La Hougue Bie
la_hougue_bie.about: La Hougue Bie in Grouville, Jersey, is a Neolithic passage grave (4000-3500 BC on Jersey Heritage's dating; French Wikipedia's radiocarbon dates from the 1991-94 excavations put the first phase c. 4365-4055 cal BC) under a great mound about 12 m high and 55-58 m across. A long, low passage, entered from the east, leads to a long chamber with side cells to north and south and a raised end compartment with a terminal cell, giving a cruciform plan; it is roofed with capstones. The tomb was closed in the later Neolithic and the cairn later covered with a clay mantle. A granite chapel, Notre Dame de la Clarté, was built on the summit in the 12th century; in the early 16th century Dean Richard Mabon added the Jerusalem Chapel with its crypt imitating the Holy Sepulchre. From 1792 Philippe d'Auvergne incorporated the chapels in the Prince's Tower, a Gothic Revival house with a round crenellated tower; it was demolished in July-August 1924 by the Société Jersiaise (owners from 1919), which then dug into the mound in September 1924 and found the tomb, entered since through a modern (concrete) tunnel. The chapels were restored (reconsecrated 1931). The original entrance and forecourt with dry-stone walls were excavated and restored in the 1990s; since then the sunrise at the equinoxes has been seen to shine along the passage to the back of the terminal cell. A German command bunker (1942) is set into the mound's flank. Quotes are exact text of the cited pages (whitespace normalised); 'derived' marks values computed from quoted numbers or OSM geometry.

clava.name: Balnuaran of Clava (Clava Cairns)
clava.record_note: Q39505213 'Balnuaran of Clava' (buildings); Q457879 'Clava cairn' is the monument type at almost the same point; place hes-SM90074 is the scheduled monument
clava.about: Balnuaran of Clava, on a gravel terrace above the River Nairn east of Inverness, is the type-site of the Clava cairns: a row of three large cairns running north-east to south-west, a passage grave at each end and a ring cairn in the middle, each with a kerb of boulders, a low rubble platform and a ring of standing stones, with a small kerb cairn to the west. The passages of the two passage graves are in line, pointing south-west to the midwinter sunset; the kerbstones and the standing stones are graded in height, tallest to the south-west, and stones were chosen for colour (red sandstone to the south-west, paler stones to the north-east). The central ring cairn has an open interior with no entrance and three stone 'rays' joining its kerb to three of the standing stones. Bradley's excavations of 1994-97 showed each monument (cairn, kerb, platform and circle) was built in one operation around 2000 BC (Early Bronze Age); the small kerb cairn and other small cairns were added about 1000 years later, when the south-west cairn was reused, and a cremation was placed by the ring cairn in the 1st millennium AD. The chambers, probably once corbelled, are now open to the sky. Fallen stones were re-erected and the cairns 'restored' by the owner in 1870-81 (a road was moved, clipping the south-west cairn, and two of its stones were moved); after Guardianship in 1925 Kathleen Kennedy cleared and tidied the cairns in 1930-31, heaping cairn material higher and making the kerbs more prominent. Quotes are exact text of the cited pages (whitespace normalised; Fraser 1884 and Barclay 1990 as their OCR reads); feet are converted at 0.3048 m and marked derived.

cites.quote: consists of a slightly oval cairn 70 by 64 ft. overall, within which a massive boulder kerb 60 by 52 ft. contains the main bulk of the structure
enclosed by a nearly circular setting of stone slabs 21 by 18 ft. across
The whole cairn stands within a circle of standing-stones with an approximate diameter of 100 ft.

These stones vary in height from 7 ft. 6 ins. to less than 1 ft., and to three of them, on the W., E. and SSE., narrow "causeways" of small pitched stones, from 6 to 8 ft. wide, run from the boulder kerb of the cairn.
On the south-south-west opposite the stump of a monolith is the most notable of the kerb-stones, a great rectangular block 4 feet 3 inches high
The cairn material is heaped up to a height of about 4 feet inside the kerb.
The central area is defined by a setting of flat slabs (in contrast to the boulders of the kerb, 2 feet 9 inches to 3 feet 6 inches high
The cairn is surrounded by nine monoliths set 25 to 21 feet outside the kerb, with an overall diameter of about 100 feet.
The tallest stone remaining is on the west-south- west and is 7 feet 6 inches high.
Its outer ring is 107 feet in diameter outside
The intermediate ring is 57 feet in diameter outside
one of them pointing to E. 10° S., another to S. 10° E., and
the third to W. 25° N.
The cairn itself is surrounded by a ring of nine standing stones (originally there were probably 11; three were re-erected in 19th century); three of these are linked to the outer kerb by stone banks
The stump of a tenth stone was revealed through visitor erosion and recorded in 1995.
There is no evidence to suggest that the chamber ever had an entrance passage or that it was roofed.
At the central ring cairn, there is evidence that the cairn, the stone circle and the external rays which connect these features together were all built at the same time.

cites.quote: The kerbstones are largest by the entrance where they are 3 feet 6 inches high.

The chamber is not exactly circular in plan, measuring 11 feet 6 inches by 13 feet in diameter.
The walls stand to a total height of 6 feet 9 inches, with a maximum of six courses of flattish but irregular stones slightly oversailing
The surrounding circle of standing stones now has ten monoliths remaining, all but four of which are known to have been reset.
The circle seems to have been set 24 to 28 feet outside the kerb.
There is an entrance to the central chamber from the south-west (S. 39° W.), 2 feet wide at the oiiter end
The outer ring is 108 feet in diameter outside, and consists at present of eleven standing stones
The intermediate ring which forms the base of the central cairn is 53 feet in diameter outside
The present height of the chamber is 7 J feet; and it would require to be 4 or 5 feet higher in order to form a complete dome.
outer ring are of the shaly sandstone flags found plentifully, in situ, in the district
The outer kerb of the south-west passage grave was originally intended to lean back into the body of cairn.
Evidence of corbelling of the central chamber survives, supporting the theory that both passage graves were originally roofed.
two rows of parallel stones are depicted on Somerville’s 1910 plan, extending along the same line as the entrance passage, beyond the outer kerb, though no trace survives.

The SW cairn, however, on the basis of its radiocarbon dates, was reused in the Late Bronze Age

elements.date: Late Bronze Age (about 1000 years after the main cairns)

lies a small circle of contiguous recumbent stone, approximately 12 feet in internal diameter
including the use of monoliths of graded height, with the tallest on the south-west arc
On the eastern side is a larger, flatter slab of red sandstone with cup-and-ring marks on its surface.
The two small ring-cairns and kerb cairn were constructed about a thousand years later and new burials placed in some of the earlier cairns.

elements.what: river-worn pebbles, quarried red sandstone slabs and glacial erratics (banded gneiss, conglomerate); kerbs of granite and gneiss boulders (Fraser); kerbstones graded and chosen for colour, larger and redder to the SW, smaller and whiter to the NE

cites.quote: The materials include a mix of river-worn pebbles, quarried red sandstone slabs, and glacial erratics (of mixed geology, including banded gneiss and conglomerates).
The kerb stones are graded in size and selected for colour, so that the stones are larger and redder to the south west, and smaller and whiter to the north east.
The visual impact of the first group is enhanced by the grading in height of the kerbstones and surrounding monoliths, creating an alignment extending from northeast to southwest

alignment.claim: The passages of the two passage graves are in line with each other and point south-west to the setting midwinter sun; the line passes two stones of the central ring cairn's circle (Thom). The grading of kerbs and circles and the stone colours emphasise the same NE-SW axis; less precisely it points to the midwinter sunrise the other way. The cairn was photographed at midwinter sunset in 1995 (Douglas Scott).

cites.quote: Both have sub-circular chambers, with entrance passages aligned towards the south-west at the point the setting midwinter sun meets the horizon
The precision of the alignment of the cairns at Balnuaran of Clava with the setting of the midwinter sun is particularly notable.
This has been connected with an alignment on the midwinter sunset and, less precisely, the midwinter sunrise.
Professor Alexander Thom discovered that the two entrance passages align exactly and that the alignment passes through two of the stones surrounding the central non-aligned cairn.
The alignment points to the midwinter sun's setting position, indicating that at some time the site perhaps had an astronomical function.
with the entrances oriented southwest towards midwinter sunset
Boyle Somerville and Euan MacKie recorded both Balnuaran of Clava passage-graves as orientated on midwinter sunset
The cairn was photographed at midwinter sunset in 1995 by Douglas Scott.

alignment.claim: Bradley suggested that midsummer sunrise linked the central ring cairn with the monument at Mains of Clava, not opposite the passages; HES describes paler mica- and quartz-rich stones sparkling in the rising midsummer sun.

whereas at midsummer, lighter coloured stones containing mica and quartz, reflect the light

cites.quote: The four large monuments forming the northern row of cairns were built around 2000BC along the line of the gravel terrace.
All proved to have been constructed during a single phase.
radiocarbon dates from Bradley’s investigations indicate that they date from about 2000 cal BC (the Early Bronze Age)

phases.name: Late Bronze Age reuse

the later and smaller cairns built around 1000 BC are set on a different axis

cites.quote: Part of the new road clipped the edge of the south-west passage grave and two monoliths were relocated.
In addition, fallen standing stones were re-erected, vegetation was cleared, and some of the cairn material was robbed to construct enclosing walls.
The three main cairns at Balnuaran of Clava were ‘restored’ by the owner, but the details of what was carried out are unclear.

phases.name: Kennedy's clearance
phases.what: vegetation and fallen stone cleared, depressions in the cairns filled and contours 'restored', kerbs exposed; over 0.3 m added to the SW cairn and its profile smoothed; kerbs made more prominent than originally

cites.quote: The site came into Guardianship on 1 June 1925.
Depressions in the Cairn (caused by the removal of cartloads of stones by road workers) were filled in, and the contour of the cairn restored.
Over 0-3 m has been added and the profile of the cairn has been very much smoothed.
It is clear that the prominent flat tops of the ramps of stone surrounding the kerb are the result of selective removal of material and that the kerbs were originally less prominent.

phases.name: Piggott's excavation
phases.what: central ring cairn interior and two trenches; kerb cairn

cites.quote: Professor Stuart Piggott conducted small-scale excavations at Balnuaran of Clava in 1953

phases.name: Bradley's excavations
phases.what: reopened Kennedy's trenches; SW cairn and ring cairn 1994, NE cairn 1995; 23 radiocarbon dates; monograph The Good Stones (SAS Monograph 17, 2000)

cites.quote: 1994-7 Archaeological excavation, field survey and recording by Professor Richard Bradley.
A total of 23 dates were obtained, with two clear clusters around the late 3rd and early 2nd millennia BC, and in the latter half of the 2nd millennium BC.
The second season of excavation (see Bradley 1994) focused on the NE passage grave

debate.claim: Dating: the passage graves were long thought Neolithic (Stone Pages still says so); Bradley's radiocarbon dates put them in the Early Bronze Age.

cites.quote: the passage graves were probably constructed in Neolithic times, and the stone circles later, during the Bronze Age
The passage graves were once thought to be Neolithic, but Bradley’s investigations at Balnuaran of Clava confirmed that they date from around 2000 cal BC.

debate.claim: Single build or not: excavation showed each monument built in one phase (Bradley 1994-95), but Bradley later argued the circles and platforms need not be of one period.

cites.quote: All proved to have been constructed during a single phase.
Bradley argues that the cairns need not be one period construction, perhaps with the circles and platforms coming later (Bradley 2016a, 116).

debate.claim: Roofing: HES and Bradley think both chambers were corbelled and roofed; Henshall and Ritchie (2001) are cautious.

cites.quote: Though Henshall and Ritchie (2001) are cautious in their interpretation of any possible roofing.
